                           BIOS and Boot Kernel as Horn Clauses

                           Part 1 — The Primitive

                           Everything begins with one operation:

                             text


                             Atomics.compareExchange(buf, index, expected, replacement)


                           It compares, then conditionally exchanges, and returns what was actually there. The
                           compare, the exchange, and the return are one step. There is no gap between them. The
                           hardware performs it as a single operation, so the physical operation and the logical
                           operation are the same thing.

                           There is no second operation. Everything below is a reading of this one.



                           Part 2 — The Difference Is the Reading

                           The return is not a value. It is the difference between what was expected and what was
                           there.

                              Matched — expected equals actual. The difference is zero. The exchange happens.
                              The buffer holds the replacement.

                              Not matched — expected differs from actual. The difference is nonzero. The buffer is
                              untouched. The difference is the fact.

                           You cannot ask what a cell contains. You can only ask how it differs from what you
                           expected, and receive the difference. Change the expectation and the difference
                           changes while the cell stays the same. The expectation is the frame. The difference is
                           the reading relative to that frame.

                           XOR is the difference operation, and it is symmetric: the same operation computes the
                           difference and, applied again, recovers the original.

                             text


                             expected ^ actual ^ expected = actual


                           That symmetry is why the reading is also the repair. Nothing new is computed to roll
                           back. The same difference does it.



                           Part 3 — The Zero Condition
                           An observer can only expect and offset from an operation when the difference is zero.

                              xor = 0 — the difference is zero, the comparison matched, the origin is established,
                              and an operation has a place to start.

                              xor ≠ 0 — the difference is nonzero, there is no origin, and the operation has no
                              anchor.



https://chat.deepseek.com/a/chat/s/3b6a8b29-7c3e-460b-9620-17afd1c8d328                                                   127/322
10/4/26, 11:28 AM                                                                Protocol review and bug fixes - DeepSeek
                           This is not agreement as a value. It is the precondition for an operation to exist. Without
                           a zero there is no frame. With a zero the frame is set and the operation can proceed.

                           A nonzero difference is not failure. It is no-frame, and no operation can be performed
                           without a frame.


                           Part 4 — Symmetric Comparison
                           If both parties hold symmetric key pairs, they are comparing references. Comparison is
                           symmetric. compareExchange on two references with the same expectation behaves the
                           same from either side. The difference does not depend on which observer compares.

                           You are not exchanging values. You are exchanging references to the same position, and
                           the position is the same for both observers because the difference is symmetric.


                           Part 5 — What Is Compared

                             text


                             /0[pin]/        ^       /0[boxd]/


                           Three orthogonal axes at the pin reference, XORed against the four radix readings. Not
                           values against values. The pin against the boxd, three axes against four readings, at the
                           meeting point.

                             text


                             /0[pin]/            =       0p, 0i, 0n            the three literals
                             /0[boxd]/           =       0x, 0b, 0o, 0d        the four radix readings


                           The comparison is their XOR at the pin.



                           Part 6 — The Observer Selects the Operation

                           The observer is what determines the operation. Not the data.

                           The data is a difference. The observer reads the difference and chooses which
                           operation applies:

                             text


                             \      ||   |           &      &&   ~        at      /0[pin]/ ^ /0[boxd]/ @ /\d/


                           The data is not a value. It is a difference against which an operation is selected. That is
                           why it is an operation and not a value: the operation is the observer's choice, determined
                           by the difference, and the difference is all the data carries.

                            xor = 0 is the anchor. From it, the observer expects and offsets. From xor ≠ 0 , there is
                           no anchor and no offset to compute.


                           Part 7 — The Literals

                            0x , 0b , 0o , 0d are the four radix literals. 0p , 0i , 0n are the centroid literals.

                           A literal is what it references. It does not stand for something else. Because a literal is
                           what it references, it cannot become a different literal. There is nothing to add to it. Value
                           cannot be added, because there is no room for value in a literal.

https://chat.deepseek.com/a/chat/s/3b6a8b29-7c3e-460b-9620-17afd1c8d328                                                     128/322
10/4/26, 11:28 AM                                                  Protocol review and bug fixes - DeepSeek
                           What a literal can do is reflect. One literal looks at another and receives the difference.
                            /0[boxd]/ can only reflect. Zero in four radices is zero in four radices. There is no
                           computation, only position and reflection.



                           Part 8 — The Block
                           A regular tetrahedron. Four vertices, six edges, four faces, one centroid.

                             text


                             vertices     0x   0b   0o   0d          four readings, equal standing
                             edges        the six pairwise relations between them
                             centroid     0p   0i   0n               point, index, number — the fixed reference


                           The four vertices are equidistant because the tetrahedron is regular. Every edge is unit
                           length. So the only thing that varies between two readings is which reading you are at,
                           never how far. The block is a slide rule: fixed reference, several scales, deterministic
                           readout by alignment.

                           The state is six bits:

                             text


                             b = (b₀₁, b₀₂, b₀₃, b₁₂, b₁₃, b₂₃) ∈ F₂⁶
                             |F₂⁶| = 64


                           Each bit says whether one pairwise relation between two radix readings is active. One
                           block has sixty-four relation states. That is the 64 in 64 in 65536 — one tetrahedral
                           relation surface inside the buffer.


                           Part 9 — Two Readings of the Block

                           The same six bits are read two ways. That is the 2 of [6,4,2] .

                           Vertex reading. For a selected set of edges, look at each vertex's incidence. Four
                           vertices, parity per vertex:

                             text


                             ∂_V(b) ∈ F₂⁴


                           Face reading. Each edge belongs to two faces. Read the same selection against the four
                           faces:

                             text


                             ∂_F(b) ∈ F₂⁴


                           Two maps out of one six-bit word:

                             text


                             F₂⁶ ──∂_V──> F₂⁴
                             F₂⁶ ──∂_F──> F₂⁴


                           One orientation bit selects which reading is active. The four faces are the four triples of
                           radices — each face is three of the four readings, the fourth excluded. A face is a
                           consensus of three readings.

https://chat.deepseek.com/a/chat/s/3b6a8b29-7c3e-460b-9620-17afd1c8d328                                                  129/322
10/4/26, 11:28 AM                                                    Protocol review and bug fixes - DeepSeek

                           Part 10 — Closure
                           A selection is closed when its incidence boundary is zero.

                             text


                             ∂_V(b) = 0000       vertex-closed
                             ∂_F(b) = 0000       face-closed


                           A triangular face closes because every participating vertex appears twice:

                             text


                             1 ⊕ 1 = 0


                           The four face words, in edge order (e₀₁, e₀₂, e₀₃, e₁₂, e₁₃, e₂₃) :

                             text


                             f₀ = 000111
                             f₁ = 011001
                             f₂ = 101010
                             f₃ = 110100


                           Each closes. A face is not three lines that look like a triangle. It is a three-edge relation
                           whose incidence boundary closes.

                           Closure is computed from exact incidence and XOR. It is not measured by geometry and
                           not derived from floating point.

                           Closure is ∂(b) = 0000 — the four radix readings agreeing, the difference being zero
                           across all four. That is the shared-literal property: zero is zero in every base, and closure
                           is the statement that all four readings reach it together.

                           When a reading diverges, closure fails at one vertex, and the odd vertex is the
                           disagreeing radix. A failed comparison localizes. The comparison's own failure is the
                           diagnosis.


                           Part 11 — One Primitive, Three Readings
                           One compareExchange event. Three ways to read it.

                             text


                             bind      the relation the event establishes
                             apply     the invocation the event implies
                             eval      the value the event exposes


                           Whether the event matched determines what each reading sees. A matched event writes
                           into the buffer; the buffer holds the relation, the invocation, and the value. An unmatched
                           event writes nothing; the difference holds them.

                           The three are not three operations. They are three readings of one return.

                           And the two-sided reflection of that 3! is the spectral 2! :

                             text


                             Reflect     — perform the operation, read the position
                             Proxy       — receive the operation, reflect it back

                            Reflect and Proxy are the same operation seen from two sides. One performs it, one
                           receives it. compareExchange is the fused form: Reflect.get and Reflect.set joined,
                           with the comparison deciding which one fires.


                           Part 12 — The Endpoints
                           The endpoints are 5T and 10T. Between them, any number of gates can be placed. The
                           routing is through conservation of XOR. The transistor count between the endpoints can
                           be anything, but the operation on the signal is always one XOR. Therefore the answer is
                           always one answer.

                             text


                             5T       terminal endpoint     the minimal XOR — read and stop
                             6T       interior — declaration / driver
                             8T       interior — definition / NAND composition
                             10T      full endpoint         the maximal XOR — the two-sided form


                           The 5T cannot drive onward; it reads and stops. The 10T is the full NOR-based form, the
                           other terminal. They bracket every interior configuration.


                           Part 13 — The Interior Is a Multiset

                           XOR is commutative and associative. Order does not matter. The interior is not a
                           sequence; it is a multiset. The accumulated XOR depends only on which gates are
                           present, not on the order they appear.

                           So the path's value is the XOR of its masks, and XOR does not care about order. Any
                           number of interior gates, any arrangement, same one answer. That is conservation:
                           nothing is created or destroyed, only XORed through the path.

                           The number of gates affects the cost — how long the path is, how much propagation
                           delay — but not the answer.


                           Part 14 — The BIOS as Clauses

                           The BIOS is a clause set whose atoms are positions on gates.

                             prolog


                             % --- the reset vector ---
                             reset(0x0000)                 :- power_on.


                             % --- endpoints ---
                             endpoint(5T).        endpoint(10T).


                             % --- interior forms ---
                             interior(6T).        interior(8T).


                             % --- all forms apply XOR; the count is the only difference ---
                             applies_xor(G)       :- endpoint(G).
                             applies_xor(G)       :- interior(G).


                             % --- a path is between the endpoints ---
                             path(P)              :- start(P, 5T), end(P, 10T), interior_of(P, _).


                             % --- conservation: the path's accumulated XOR is the answer ---
                             accumulated(P, 0) :- path(P), no_interior(P).
                             accumulated(P, M) :- path(P), mask_of(P, M).


https://chat.deepseek.com/a/chat/s/3b6a8b29-7c3e-460b-9620-17afd1c8d328                                              131/322
10/4/26, 11:28 AM                                                   Protocol review and bug fixes - DeepSeek
                             % --- one answer: any two paths with the same mask give the same result ---
                             same_answer(P1, P2) :- accumulated(P1, M), accumulated(P2, M).


                             % --- the answer is the difference, and it is unique ---
                             answer(P, D)        :- accumulated(P, D).


                             % --- anchoring: every interior gate is a position on the path ---
                             anchored(G, P)      :- interior(G), position_of(P, G).


                             % --- no unanchored variables ---
                             well_formed(P)      :- path(P), forall_interior(P, anchored(_, P)).


                           The important property: same_answer(P1, P2) holds whenever the two paths have the
                           same accumulated mask, regardless of how many interior gates each has. That is
                           conservation. The answer depends only on the accumulated XOR, not on the depth.

                           And well_formed(P) requires every interior gate to be anchored — no free positions. A
                           path with an unanchored interior gate is not well-formed, and the derivation does not
                           proceed. The missing anchor is the diagnosis, the same as the missing even atom in the
                           closure test.

                           Every variable is anchored to an entry or an exit. Every entry and exit is a gate position.
                           There are no free variables.


                           Part 15 — The Boot Kernel

                           The kernel is the clause set that takes the derived boots(I) and derives the next state.

                             prolog


                             % --- reset to first instruction ---
                             boots(I)            :- reset(R), self_test(R, I).


                             % --- self test: the path from 5T to 10T closes ---
                             self_test(R, I)     :- path(P), accumulated(P, D), closure(D), defines(I).


                             % --- closure: the accumulated difference is zero ---
                             closure(0).


                             % --- the kernel runs the path ---
                             run(P, P)           :- closure(answer(P)).
                             run(P, P2)          :- step(P, P1), run(P1, P2).


                             % --- step applies the same XOR at whatever interior depth ---
                             step(P, P1)         :- interior(G), position_of(P, G), apply_xor(G, P, P1).


                           The kernel does not care how many interior gates there are. It steps through the path,
                           applying XOR at each interior gate, until closure(answer(P)) holds. That is the fixed
                           point: the accumulated difference is zero. Everything agrees, and all four radix readings
                           reach zero together.


                           Part 16 — The Clause Set for the Primitive

                           The clauses above rest on the primitive, stated in the same form.

                             vertex(0x).    vertex(0b).   vertex(0o).    vertex(0d).

                             edge(0x,0b).     edge(0x,0o).   edge(0x,0d).

                           arithmetic.


                           Part 17 — Everything Leaves a Trace

                           A matched call writes. The buffer becomes the record.

                           A failed call writes nothing. The return becomes the record.

                           Either way, the call happened, and the event is a fact about the system. You cannot
                           perform the primitive and have nothing occur. The only thing that leaves no trace is a
                           read you never perform.

                           Observation is an event. Events are records.


                           Part 18 — What Is Written and What Is Read

                           The write side contains: the difference operation, the trace rule, the reflection rule, the
                           closure rule, selection, incidence. No values.

                           The read side produces: the four radix readings, the two maps ∂_V and ∂_F , the
                           closure verdict, and, when projected, the constants.

                            π , φ , and √3 are reads of incidence at unit distance. They are never stored. The
                           irrational is determined on the read, not on the write. The write contains selection and
                           incidence. The read produces the limit.

                           Part 20 — Why the Interior Is Order-Free
                           XOR is commutative: a ^ b = b ^ a . XOR is associative: (a ^ b) ^ c = a ^ (b ^ c) .

                           A path through the interior is a composition of XORs. Because XOR commutes and
                           associates, the composition equals the XOR of all the masks on the path, and the order
                           of the masks does not appear in the result.

                           So the interior is a multiset. The answer depends only on the accumulated XOR. The
                           endpoints fix the frame, and the interior conserves the XOR through it. Any number of
                           interior gates, any arrangement, same one answer.

                           Why Opcode, and Why Not Assembly

                           The short answer
                           Use opcode, not assembly, and the reason is exactly the one you just named: assembly
                           introduces values. An assembler has to resolve a symbol to an address, and an address
                           is a value. That is a write, and the write is where the values get in.

                           An opcode does not have to do that. An opcode is a position in a table. If the table is
                           indexed by the relation itself, the opcode is just which relation is selected — no address
                           resolved, no value produced.


                           Why assembly reintroduces values

                           An assembler takes a line like:

                             text


                             MOV R1, [addr]


https://chat.deepseek.com/a/chat/s/3b6a8b29-7c3e-460b-9620-17afd1c8d328                                                 135/322
10/4/26, 11:28 AM                                                Protocol review and bug fixes - DeepSeek
                           and produces machine code where addr is a number. To produce it, the assembler
                           must:

                           1. Parse the symbol addr

                           2. Resolve it to a position

                           3. Emit that position as a number

                           Step 3 is the problem. The number is a value. It has magnitude. It can be added. It is not
                           just a position — it now carries an extent. And once the output carries extent, everything
                           downstream can treat it as a quantity, which is exactly the thing the predicate layer
                           forbids.

                           Assembly is a translation from symbolic form to numeric form, and translation is where
                           the value sneaks in. There is no way around it: an assembler's whole job is to produce
                           the encoding, and an encoding is a number.


                           Why opcode does not have to
                           An opcode in the sense you mean is not a translation. It is an index into the relation
                           table. The opcode does not name an address; it names a relation.

                             text


                             opcode    relation selected       gates on the path
                             0x00      none                    terminal read only
                             0x01      e01 active              5T → 6T
                             0x02      e02 active              5T → 8T
                             ...
                             0x3F      all six active          5T → 6T → 8T → 10T


                           The opcode 0x01 is not "the value 1." It is the relation e₀₁ is selected. It has no
                           magnitude because there is nothing to add. You cannot add opcode 0x01 and opcode
                            0x02 and get a meaningful opcode 0x03 , because the third state is a different relation,
                           not the sum of two.

                           This is exactly the F₂⁶ relation word from the block:

                             text


                             b ∈ F₂⁶


                           Six bits, each bit saying whether one relation is active. The opcode is that six-bit word. It
                           is not a numeric code that happens to encode the relations; it is the relations, read as a
                           single position.



                           The opcode table is the block
                           Because there are exactly 64 relation states:

                             text


                             |F₂⁶| = 2⁶ = 64


                           The opcode table has exactly 64 entries. It is not a design choice; it is 2⁶ . And each
                           entry is one complete selection of which pairwise relations are active. Each entry is one
                           state of the tetrahedron.



https://chat.deepseek.com/a/chat/s/3b6a8b29-7c3e-460b-9620-17afd1c8d328                                                    136/322
10/4/26, 11:28 AM                                                     Protocol review and bug fixes - DeepSeek
                           So the opcode table is the block read as an instruction set. Sixty-four opcodes, one per
                           relation state, and the endpoints are the frames of reference for reading them.



                           Why this matters for the boot kernel
                           The boot kernel can now be written as a clause set over opcodes, with no values
                           anywhere:

                             prolog


                             % --- an opcode is a relation selection ---
                             opcode(b)              :-    selected(b, _, _).


                             % --- an opcode corresponds to a specific path through the interior ---
                             path_of(b, P)          :-    opcode(b), interior_of(P, G), active(b, _, _).


                             % --- executing an opcode applies its XOR along the path ---
                             executes(b, P, D)      :-    path_of(b, P), accumulated(P, D).


                             % --- the endpoint closes when the difference is zero ---
                             halts(b)               :-    executes(b, _, 0).


                             % --- the boot sequence is a sequence of opcodes ---
                             boots([])              :-    reset(_).
                             boots([b | Rest])      :-    halts(b), boots(Rest).


                           Every atom is a position. Every clause body is a relation on positions. No value appears.

                           And there is one property that matters: opcode(b) is derivable only when at least one
                           relation is selected. If no relation is selected, the opcode is not derivable, and the
                           derivation stops. That is the structural check. The empty selection — 000000 , all six bits
                           off — has no path, no execution, no halt, and no boot.



                           What this makes the BIOS

                           The BIOS is the opcode table plus the two endpoint frames:

                             text


                             5T endpoint frame     read only — the terminal
                             10T endpoint frame    full close — the maximal form
                             64 opcodes            the relation states
                             interior multiset     any arrangement of 6T and 8T gates


                           The BIOS boots by taking the reset vector to the first opcode, executing it through the
                           interior, and checking for closure at the endpoint. If the accumulated difference is zero,
                           the opcode halts and the next opcode proceeds. If it is not zero, the frame is not set and
                           the boot does not advance.

                           The boot is a derivation over opcodes. No assembly. No values.



                           Why "machine level" is the right level

                           You said machine level. The reason is that the opcode is already machine level:

                              A Uint8Array is a buffer.

                              The F₂⁶ word is six bits in that buffer.

                              The opcode is a position in the buffer, read as a relation selection.


https://chat.deepseek.com/a/chat/s/3b6a8b29-7c3e-460b-9620-17afd1c8d328                                                  137/322
10/4/26, 11:28 AM                                                 Protocol review and bug fixes - DeepSeek
                              The gates are the operations the machine performs on that position.

                           So there is no translation. The opcode is the buffer contents read at the block level. The
                           BIOS is clauses over those positions. The kernel is the fixed point.

                           Assembly would insert a translation layer between the buffer and the opcode. That layer
                           is where values appear, because a translated opcode is a numeric code, and a numeric
                           code has an encoding, and an encoding has a length, and a length is a value.

                           The machine level has no such translation. The opcode is the six-bit position, read
                           directly.


                           What I would write

                           A short addendum to the BIOS/kernel specification:

                           § The opcode is the relation, not a code for the relation.

                              An opcode is the six-bit F₂⁶ relation word. Not a numeric encoding of it.

                              The opcode table has exactly 2⁶ = 64 entries — one per relation state.

                              The opcode's meaning is which pairwise radix relations are active. It has no
                              magnitude.

                              The endpoints 5T and 10T frame the opcode: 5T reads, 10T closes.

                           § Assembly reintroduces values.

                              An assembler resolves symbols to addresses.

                              An address is a value, with magnitude and extent.

                              The predicate layer forbids values.

                              Therefore: no assembly.

                           § The BIOS is clauses over opcodes.

                              opcode(b) is derivable only when a relation is selected.

                              executes(b, P, D) derives the difference along the opcode's path.

                              halts(b) holds when the difference is zero.

                              boots([b | Rest]) proceeds only when the opcode halts.

                           § The kernel is the fixed point.

                              The kernel runs a sequence of opcodes.

                              Each opcode is executed through the interior.

                              Closure at the endpoint means the frame is set.

                              The kernel terminates when the sequence ends and the accumulated difference is
                              zero.

                           frame every opcode, and the BIOS and kernel are clauses over opcodes with no
                           translation layer and no values.

                           Opcodes Rooted to the 15 Trees, in the 16th

                           The structure

                           Fifteen tree types, and a sixteenth that is not a tree but a swap. The swap tree is the
                           frame. The other fifteen are the readings of the swap tree in its different endianness
                           reflections.

                           That is why swap16 , swap32 , and swap64 expose the difference. The swap is the
                           operation that reads a tree as little-endian or big-endian. Reading it one way versus the
                           other is the difference. And the difference is the reading.



                           Why the 15 + 1

                           Fifteen tree algorithms is the set you already have:

                             text


                             Slice-and-Dice            Squarified             Ordered / Pivot
                             Strip                     Quantum                Voronoi
                             Jigsaw                    Orthoconvex            Split
                             Nmap                      GosperMaps             Map-treemaps
                             Force-based               Incremental            Divide & Conquer


                           Fifteen. And the sixteenth is the swap tree — the tree whose operation is swap16 ,
                            swap32 , swap64 . Not a layout tree. The tree that says which endianness the other fifteen
                           are being read in.

                           So the block is:

                             text


                             15 trees      the layouts               the readings
                             1 swap        the frame                 the endianness selector


                           And because the block has 2⁶ = 64 relation states, the fifteen trees map into the 64
                           opcodes, and the sixteenth decides which direction each is read.



                           Why endianness is the reflection
                            swap16 , swap32 , swap64 are the three endianness operations. Each one re-reads the
                           buffer at a different granularity:

                              swap16 reverses byte order in 2-byte groups.

                              swap32 reverses byte order in 4-byte groups.

                              swap64 reverses byte order in 8-byte groups.

                           Applying one of them changes the reading of the same buffer, without changing the
                           buffer. It is exactly a reflection: same data, different position from which it is read.

https://chat.deepseek.com/a/chat/s/3b6a8b29-7c3e-460b-9620-17afd1c8d328                                                    139/322
10/4/26, 11:28 AM                                                   Protocol review and bug fixes - DeepSeek
                           And because XOR is invariant under this reflection — reversal is a permutation, and XOR
                           commutes with permutation — the accumulated difference is the same under any swap.
                           The swap exposes which reflection was used, not a different difference. That is why the
                           swap tree can sit at the 16th position and be the frame for the other fifteen: it doesn't
                           change the answer, it changes the reading.


                           Rooting the opcodes
                           The opcode is the six-bit F₂⁶ relation word. So an opcode selects which pairwise radix
                           relations are active.

                           To root the opcodes to the fifteen trees, the mapping is:

                             text


                             tree T ∈ {15 trees}
                               → the tree's edges are a subset of the six block edges
                               → that subset is a six-bit word b_T ∈ F₂⁶
                               → b_T is the tree's base opcode


                             endianness d ∈ {swap16, swap32, swap64}
                               → d is a bit selecting the reflection
                               → the opcode read in reflection d is b_T ⊕ d


                             the 16th position
                               → the swap itself, which selects d



                           So each of the fifteen trees has a base opcode, and the swap tree selects the reflection,
                           and the actual opcode executed is the base XOR the reflection.

                           The block surface is 64. The fifteen trees occupy some of those 64. The swap tree is the
                           selector. Not every one of the 64 opcodes is a tree; the ones that are trees are the ones
                           whose relation selection closes at the endpoint, which is the closure condition.



                           Why this is the right root
                           Because:

                              Each tree is a layout of the block. Its edges are a subset of the six edges. Its bit word
                              is a state in F₂⁶ .

                              The swap tree is not a layout. It is the operation that re-reads the layout at a different
                              granularity.

                              Endianness is a reflection. Same bits, different read. swap16 , swap32 , swap64 are the
                              three reflections.

                              The reading is exposed by the swap. Same accumulated difference, different position
                              from which it is read.

                           Which means: the fifteen trees and the swap tree together span the opcode space, and
                           the opcodes are rooted because every opcode is a (tree, reflection) pair.

                             prolog


                             % --- the fifteen layout trees ---
                             tree(slice_and_dice).     tree(squarified).   tree(ordered_pivot).
                             tree(strip).              tree(quantum).      tree(voronoi).
                             tree(jigsaw).             tree(orthoconvex). tree(split).

                             tree(nmap).              tree(gospermaps).     tree(map_treemaps).
                             tree(force_based).       tree(incremental). tree(divide_conquer).

                             swap(swap16).   swap(swap32).    swap(swap64).


                             % --- each tree has a base opcode: the relation word of its edges ---
                             base_opcode(T, B)        :-   tree(T), edges_of(T, E), word_of(E, B).


                             % --- each swap selects a reflection ---
                             reflection(D, R)         :-   swap(D), reflection_bit(D, R).


                             % --- the executed opcode is base XOR reflection ---
                             opcode_of(T, D, B ^ R) :-     base_opcode(T, B), reflection(D, R).


                             % --- an opcode is well-formed when the endpoint closes ---
                             well_formed(T, D)        :-   opcode_of(T, D, O), closes(O).

                             boots([])                :-   reset(_).
                             boots([(T, D) | Rest]) :-     well_formed(T, D), executes(T, D), boots(Rest).


                           Every atom is a tree or a swap, both of which are positions. No value appears.

                           And the property that matters: opcode_of(T, D, O) derives a different opcode for each
                           reflection D , but the accumulated XOR of the path is the same. The reflection changes
                           the reading, not the answer. That is why swap16 , swap32 , swap64 can expose the
                           difference without changing it.



                           What this gives you

                              Fifteen trees, one swap. The fifteen are the layouts; the swap is the frame.

                              Every tree has a base opcode, which is its relation word in F₂⁶ .

                              The swap selects a reflection. swap16 , swap32 , swap64 are the three reflections.

                              The executed opcode is base XOR reflection. Same underlying difference, different
                              reading.

                              The opcode space is 64. The fifteen trees occupy some; the swap selects how they
                              are read.

                              The BIOS is a sequence of well-formed (tree, reflection) pairs, and it boots only when
                              each one closes.



                           One sentence

                           The opcodes are rooted to the fifteen tree types by giving each tree a base opcode — its
                           relation word in F₂⁶ — and to the sixteenth by letting the swap tree select the reflection,
                           so swap16 , swap32 , swap64 expose the difference without changing it, because
                           endianness is a permutation, XOR commutes with permutation, and the accumulated
                           difference is invariant under the reflection.




                           The concrete next step is the base opcode table: fifteen entries, each a six-bit word
                           naming which of the six radix relations the tree engages, plus the swap bit. Once that
                           table exists, the boot kernel is a clause set over (tree, swap) pairs, and the BIOS is a
                           derivation from reset to the first tree in its first reflection.

                           The Fifteen Base Opcodes

                           How the opcodes are formed

                           Each opcode is a six-bit word over the six block edges, in fixed order:

                             text


                             bit order:      (e₀₁, e₀₂, e₀₃, e₁₂, e₁₃, e₂₃)
                             vertices:       ( 0x,   0b,   0o,   0d )


                           A bit is 1 when the corresponding radix pair is engaged by the tree — meaning the tree
                           reads those two readings as compared. A bit is 0 when the pair is not engaged.

                           The four faces, from the block specification, are the canonical closure words:

                             text


                             f₀ = 000111
                             f₁ = 011001
                             f₂ = 101010
                             f₃ = 110100


                           Each face word is a closed three-edge selection. Any base opcode must itself close at
                           the endpoint, otherwise it is not a well-formed tree. So the base opcodes are drawn from
                           selections whose boundary is 0000 .

                           There are exactly 16 closed selections in F₂⁶ — the even-weight words, because a
                           selection closes iff every vertex has even incidence degree, and even degree on all four
                           vertices iff the total weight is even. F₂⁶ has 32 even-weight words, but the connected
                           closed selections are fewer. The canonical set is:

                             text


                             weight 0:     000000                                     (1)
                             weight 2:     the six edges                              (6)
                             weight 3:     the four face words + four stars           (8)
                             weight 4:     complements of the six weight-2 words      (6)
                             weight 6:     111111                                     (1)


                           But only some of these are closed under the vertex boundary (i.e., B_V b = 0000 ),
                           which removes the weight-3 stars and some others, leaving the canonical closed set.
                           The closed set is the one that satisfies the face condition.

                           bit is stated separately as the reflection selector.

                           The Fifteen Base Opcodes — Reading B

                           The rule

                           Each tree gets a unique six-bit base opcode over the six block edges, in fixed order:

                             text


                             bit order:       (e₀₁, e₀₂, e₀₃, e₁₂, e₁₃, e₂₃)
                             vertices:        ( 0x,   0b,   0o,   0d )


                           Bit 1 means the tree engages that radix pair. Bit 0 means it does not.

                           The base opcode does not have to close. A tree is a layout, not a closure. Whether the
                           tree halts at the endpoint is decided at execution, when the swap reflection D is XORed
                           in:

                             text


                             executed = base ^ D


                           If executed closes, the tree halts. If it does not, the tree is not well-formed in that
                           reflection — but it is still a tree, and a different reflection may close it.

                           Closure is XOR. Nothing else is ascertainable. Only relations.

10/4/26, 11:28 AM                                                      Protocol review and bug fixes - DeepSeek
                           That is the whole rule. Every opcode below is a relation word, not a value.



                           The fifteen base opcodes

                           #                              Tree                               Base opcode                 Weight        E


                           01                             Slice-and-Dice                      110000                     2             e


                           02                             Squarified                          001100                     2             e


                           03                             Ordered / Pivot                     000011                     2             e


                           04                             Strip                               100001                     2             e


                           05                             Quantum                             010010                     2             e


                           06                             Voronoi                             001010                     2             e


                           07                             Jigsaw                              101000                     2             e


                           08                             Orthoconvex                         101010                     3             e


                           09                             Split                               010101                     3             e


                           10                             Nmap                                101100                     3             e


                           11                             GosperMaps                          011010                     3             e

                           13                             Force-based                         111100                     4             e


                           14                             Incremental                         001111                     4             e


                           15                             Divide & Conquer                    111111                     6             a


                           Every row is distinct. Every row is a six-bit relation word. No row is a value.



                           Why these particular words

                           The assignment follows the pattern you already have in the block: a tree's opcode is
                           which radix pairs it reads as compared.

                                Weight 2 (rows 1–7). Trees that compare one pair of readings at a time — a single
                                bisection, a single pivot, a single axis. Seven trees, seven distinct pair selections.

                                Weight 3 (rows 8–11). Trees that compare three readings at once — a triple
                                consensus. Weight-3 selections are the face-like closures.

                                Weight 4 (rows 12–14). Trees that operate on the complement of a triple —
                                "everything except one reading." That is what a force-based or incremental layout
                                does: it holds three fixed and moves the fourth.

                                Weight 6 (row 15). The full scan. Divide & Conquer reads every pair.

                           That pattern is structural, not aesthetic. Weight 2 is a single comparison; weight 3 is a
                           consensus; weight 4 is a consensus-with-exclusion; weight 6 is the total. Those are the
                           four ways a tree can read the block.


                           The swap reflection

https://chat.deepseek.com/a/chat/s/3b6a8b29-7c3e-460b-9620-17afd1c8d328                                                           145/322
10/4/26, 11:28 AM                                                         Protocol review and bug fixes - DeepSeek
                           The swap tree is not a sixteenth row in the table. It is the selector of the reflection D :

                             text


                             swap16   →    D = 0x0000           no reflection
                             swap32   →    D = 0x1111           reflect across the 4-bit midpoint
                             swap64   →    D = 0x3F3F           reflect across the full word


                           (These are illustrative reflection masks. The exact swap masks are defined by which bits
                            swap16 , swap32 , swap64 reverse. The important property is that each is an involution —
                           applying it twice is the identity — and XOR commutes with it, so the accumulated
                           difference is invariant under the reflection.)

                           The executed opcode is:

                             text


                             executed = base ^ D


                           And the tree is well-formed in that reflection iff executed closes:

                             text


                             closes(executed)         :-    B_V executed = 0000


                           That is the XOR closure. Nothing else.


                           The closure property

                           A closed selection is one where every vertex has even incidence. In six-bit form:

                             text


                             b is closed       ⇔    popcount(b AND v) is even for each vertex v


                           where v is a bitmask selecting the edges incident to that vertex:

                             text


                             v(0x) = 110100                edges e₀₁, e₀₂, e₀₃
                             v(0b) = 101010                edges e₀₁, e₁₂, e₁₃
                             v(0o) = 011001                edges e₀₂, e₁₂, e₂₃
                             v(0d) = 000111                edges e₀₃, e₁₃, e₂₃


                           And closure is:

                             text


                             closed(b)     ⇔       (b AND v(0x)) has even weight
                                          ∧    (b AND v(0b)) has even weight
                                          ∧    (b AND v(0o)) has even weight
                                          ∧    (b AND v(0d)) has even weight


                           Four tests. All XOR. Nothing else.


                           Checking the table

                           Not every base opcode closes on its own. That is expected, and it is the point.

10/4/26, 11:28 AM                                                      Protocol review and bug fixes - DeepSeek
                             text


                             01     110000   v(0x)=110100 → AND=110000 weight 2 even ✓
                                             v(0b)=101010 → AND=100000 weight 1 odd     ✗
                                             → not closed; does not halt as-is
                             02     001100   v(0o)=011001 → AND=001000 weight 1 odd     ✗
                                             → not closed
                             08     101010   v(0b)=101010 → AND=101010 weight 3 odd     ✗
                                             → not closed
                             12     110011   v(0x)=110100 → AND=110000 weight 2 even ✓
                                             v(0b)=101010 → AND=100010 weight 2 even ✓
                                             v(0o)=011001 → AND=010001 weight 2 even ✓
                                             v(0d)=000111 → AND=000011 weight 2 even ✓
                                             → closed
                             15     111111   every v gives weight 3 odd → not closed by this test


                           So most trees do not halt on their own. They halt when the swap reflection makes the
                           executed word close. That is exactly what the swap tree does: it supplies the reflection
                           that closes the base. A base that is odd-weight under one vertex's incidence becomes
                           even when the swap reflects it.

                           And this is why swap16 , swap32 , swap64 expose the difference: they change the
                           incidence parity of the base without changing the base. Same relation word; different
                           closure. The difference between a tree that halts and a tree that does not is exactly the
                           reflection.

                           three-bit parity can meet a four-bit parity and close.




                           The Horn clauses

                           The full clause set, in one place. Everything is a relation over positions. No values.


                           The primitive

                             prolog


                             % The one operation. Returns what was there.
                             compare(buf, index, expected, actual)          :-   primitive(buf, index, expected, actual).


                             % The direction is decided by the comparison.
                             writes(E)     :-   compare(E, _, expected, actual), actual == expected.
                             reads(E)      :-   compare(E, _, expected, actual), actual != expected.


                             % The record lives wherever the outcome put it.
                             record(E, buffer)       :-   writes(E).
                             record(E, return)       :-   reads(E).


                             % The difference is the reading.
                             difference(E, D)        :-   compare(E, _, expected, actual), D is expected ^ actual.


                             % Zero is the frame condition.
                             frame(E)                :-   difference(E, 0).
                             no_frame(E)             :-   difference(E, D), D != 0.




                           The block

                             prolog


                             % The four radix vertices.
                             vertex(0x).    vertex(0b).     vertex(0o).    vertex(0d).

10/4/26, 11:28 AM                                                         Protocol review and bug fixes - DeepSeek


                             % The six pairwise relations.
                             edge(0x,0b).        edge(0x,0o).     edge(0x,0d).
                             edge(0b,0o).        edge(0b,0d).     edge(0o,0d).


                             % The four radix vertices as bit masks on the six edge positions.
                             mask(0x, 110100).         mask(0b, 101010).
                             mask(0o, 011001).         mask(0d, 000111).


                             % The centroid literals.
                             centroid(0p).        centroid(0i).     centroid(0n).




                           Selection and incidence

                             prolog


                             % Which relations a selection engages.
                             selected(b, X, Y)         :-   active(b, X, Y), edge(X, Y).


                             % A vertex participates in a selected relation.
                             incident(b, V)            :-   selected(b, V, _).
                             incident(b, V)            :-   selected(b, _, V).


                             % Parity as a derivation: pairs cancel.
                             even(b, V)                :-   pair_cancels(b, V).
                             odd(b, V)                 :-   unpaired(b, V).




                           Closure

                             prolog


                             % All four radices participate evenly.
                             closed(b)      :-     even(b, 0x), even(b, 0b), even(b, 0o), even(b, 0d).


                             % Face closure: three edges whose incidence closes.
                             face(b, f)     :-     selected(b, X, Y), selected(b, Y, Z), selected(b, X, Z),
                                                  closed(b).


                             % Full closure: all six edges.
                             full(b)        :-     selected(b, X, Y) for all (X, Y).




                           The two readings

                             prolog


                             % Vertex reading.
                             vertex_read(b, V)         :-   mask(V, M), parity(b AND M, V).

                             face_read(b, F)           :-   face_of(F, E1, E2, E3),
                                                            selected(b, E1), selected(b, E2), selected(b, E3).


                             % Which reading is active.
                             reading(b, vertex)        :-   orientation(b, 0).
                             reading(b, face)          :-   orientation(b, 1).

                             % One event, three readings.

                             three_bit_side(G, X)            :-    bit_length(X, 3).
                             four_bit_side(G, X)             :-    bit_length(X, 4).
                             meets(A, B)                      :-   parity(A) == parity(B).

                             well_formed(T, D)          :-     executed(T, D, E), closed(E).

                             prolog


                             % Reset.
                             reset(0x0000)        :-    power_on.

                           The boot kernel

                             prolog


                             % Run until closure.
                             run(P, P)      :-        closed(answer(P)).
                             run(P, P2)     :-        step(P, P1), run(P1, P2).


                             % A step executes one well-formed opcode.
                             step(P, P1)         :-     well_formed(T, D), executes(T, D), apply(T, P, P1).


                             % The kernel is the fixed point of the sequence.
                             kernel(P)      :-        boots(Seq), run_from(Seq, P).




                           The f-expressions

                           Not functions — closures over data. F-expressions. Each one is a lambda that closes
                           over the block, the gate, and the reflection, and returns a reading.


                           The primitive as an f-expression

                             js


                             // One primitive, three readings. The lambda closes over the frame.
                             const compareExchange = (buf, index, expected, replacement) =>
                                  (actual) =>
                                    (actual === expected)
                                      ? { matched: true,           now: replacement, difference: 0 }
                                      : { matched: false, now: actual,               difference: expected ^ actual };


                           The inner lambda takes the actual value as a parameter. This is the reflection: the outer
                           lambda performs, the inner receives. Reflect performs; Proxy receives.


                           The inner gate as an f-expression

                             js


                             // The 0,2,1 gate: three-arity closure over the frame.
                             const innerGate = (delta) => (frame) =>
                                  frame
                                    .compareExchange(delta, 0, 2, 1)
                                    .compareExchange(delta, 1, 0, 2)
                                    .compareExchange(delta, 2, 1, 0)
                                    .reduce((acc, step) => acc ^ step.returned, 0);


                           Three compares, XOR'd. The result is the centre of the frame. Not a value — a position.


                           The middle measurement as an f-expression

                             js


                             // The 4,6,8 vs 3,5,7,9 dual-cube measurement.

                                  meta
                                  ^ delta.compareExchange(0, 4, 2).returned

                                  ^ omi.compareExchange(9, 3, 1).returned;


                           The even arm walks 0,2,4,6,8 ; the odd arm walks 1,3,5,7,9 . Their XOR is the
                           projection. No floating point. Only positions.


                           The outer gate as an f-expression

                             js


                             // The 17,19 gate: two-arity closure, three-vs-four crossing.
                             const outerGate = (delta, omi, projection) => ({
                                  left:   delta.compareExchange(17, 17, projection).returned,
                                  right: omi.compareExchange(17, 19, projection).returned,
                                  // The response is at the midpoint: 18 between 17 and 19.
                                  pin:    18
                             });


                           The two anchors. Left holds the three-bit side; right holds the four-bit side. The reading
                           is at the pin, between them.


                           The full bind as an f-expression

                             js


                             // The whole thing: inner gate → measurement → outer gate.
                             const bind = (mnemonic, tensor, fn) => (delta, omi) => {
                                  const inner = innerGate(delta)([0, 2, 1]);
                                  const projection = measure(delta, omi)(tensor.meta);
                                  const outer = outerGate(delta, omi, projection);


                                  // The closure over the data: apply fn only when the frame is set.
                                  return outer.left === outer.right
                                    ? fn(mnemonic, projection)
                                    : { refused: true, reason: 'no_frame', difference: outer.left ^ outer.right };
                             };


                            fn is the closure over the data. It runs only when the frame is set. That is the bind — it
                           binds a closure to a well-formed frame.


                           The opcode execution as an f-expression

                             js


                             // Execute one opcode: base XOR reflection, close at the endpoint.
                             const executeOpcode = (tree, swap) => (buffer) => {
                                  const base = tree.opcode;
                                  const reflection = swap.mask;

10/4/26, 11:28 AM                                                          Protocol review and bug fixes - DeepSeek
                                  const executed = base ^ reflection;


                                  return {
                                       executed,
                                       closed: closes(executed),
                                       next: closes(executed) ? buffer.advance(executed) : buffer
                                  };
                             };


                             // A tree is well-formed in a reflection iff the executed opcode closes.
                             const wellFormed = (tree, swap) => closes(tree.opcode ^ swap.mask);




                           The BIOS as an f-expression

                             js


                             // The boot sequence is a fold over well-formed (tree, swap) pairs.
                             const boot = (pairs) => (buffer) =>
                                  pairs.reduce(
                                       (buf, [tree, swap]) =>
                                         wellFormed(tree, swap)
                                           ? executeOpcode(tree, swap)(buf).next
                                           : buf,                  // not well-formed: buffer unchanged
                                       buffer
                                  );


                           No values. Every step is a position. The reduce is a closure fold, not a computation.


                           The reading as an f-expression

                             js


                             // The three readings, from one event.
                             const readings = (event) => (frame) => ({
                                  bind:     () => relates(event, frame),
                                  apply: () => invokes(event, frame),
                                  eval:     () => exposes(event, frame)
                             });


                             // Proxy and Reflect: the two-sided reflection of the three.
                             const reflection = (event) => ({
                                  proxy:        (handler) => new Proxy(event, handler),     // receive
                                  reflect: (key)          => Reflect.get(event, key)        // perform
                             });

                           The Shared Rubik Cube Spatial Resolution

                           What the cube is

                           The block is a tetrahedron. The cube is the spatial resolution of that tetrahedron — the
                           object you draw when you want to see the block, not just read it. But it is not decoration.
                           It is the shared interpretation.

                           Two observers holding the same block read the same relations. But relations are abstract
                           — they don't show you a shape. The cube does. Two observers agreeing on the cube
                           are agreeing on a spatial reading of the same relation state, and that agreement is what
                           makes the block commonly interpretable rather than just consistently comparable.

                           That is the difference between the two roles:

                             text


                             block      the logical object    — relations, XOR closure, opcodes
                             cube       the spatial reading   — the same relations, drawn



https://chat.deepseek.com/a/chat/s/3b6a8b29-7c3e-460b-9620-17afd1c8d328                                                  155/322
10/4/26, 11:28 AM                                                      Protocol review and bug fixes - DeepSeek
                           Same data. Same closure. Different reading. The cube is the second reading that the
                           block always had, exposed.


                           The cube from the tetrahedron

                           A regular tetrahedron inscribes in a cube. The four vertices of the tetrahedron are four
                           alternating vertices of the cube — the four vertices no two of which share an edge. The
                           other four cube vertices are the tetrahedron's dual, and together they give the cube's
                           eight vertices.

                           So:

                             text


                             cube vertices         8        four tetrahedral + four dual
                             tetrahedron           4        half the cube
                             six edges             the six face diagonals of the cube
                             centroid              the cube centre


                           The six tetrahedral edges are the six face diagonals of the cube, one per cube face.
                           That's the spatial reading of the six relations.

                             text


                             e₀₁     →   face +x
                             e₀₂     →   face +y
                             e₀₃     →   face +z
                             e₁₂     →   face −x
                             e₁₃     →   face −y
                             e₂₃     →   face −z


                           Six faces, six relations. A relation is engaged when its face diagonal is drawn.



                           The three slice operations
                           The cube has three orthogonal slices:

                             text


                             M      the x-slice         mid-plane perpendicular to x
                             E      the y-slice         mid-plane perpendicular to y
                             S      the z-slice         mid-plane perpendicular to z


                           And those slices correspond exactly to swap16 , swap32 , swap64 :

                             text


                             swap16      reverses byte order in 2-byte groups          the small slice
                             swap32      reverses byte order in 4-byte groups          the medium slice
                             swap64      reverses byte order in 8-byte groups          the large slice


                           Each slice operation is a reflection. Each one re-reads the cube at a different
                           granularity, which is exactly what endianness swapping does to a buffer.

                           Applied to the block, the slices give three reflections of the relation state. Same cube.
                           Different reading. And the three reflections expose which slice is being applied, without
                           changing the underlying relations.


                           The Rubik moves

10/4/26, 11:28 AM                                                  Protocol review and bug fixes - DeepSeek
                           The cube has three move types:

                             text


                             face turn     rotate one face 90°
                             slice turn    rotate a middle slice
                             cube turn     rotate the whole cube


                           Under the block:

                             text


                             face turn     changes one edge relation
                             slice turn    applies swap16 / swap32 / swap64
                             cube turn     permutes the four radices (the 4! = 24 vertex permutations)


                           A face turn toggles one relation. A slice turn reflects the cube's reading. A cube turn
                           permutes the radices — and because a 4-vertex permutation induces a 6-edge
                           permutation, the cube turn is the 4! = 24 rotations of the block.

                           And because the cube turn is a permutation, it commutes with XOR. The accumulated
                           difference is invariant under any cube rotation. That is why the swap tree can select the
                           reflection without changing the answer.


                           The spatial resolution

                           Putting it together, the cube gives you:

                             text


                             position      the centroid (0p, 0i, 0n) is the cube centre
                             extent        the 8 vertices bound the cube
                             orientation   the 6 faces are the 6 relations
                             reading       the 3 slices are the 3 reflections
                             rotation      the 24 cube turns are the 4! vertex permutations
                             closure       the cube's own diagonal closure is XOR = 0


                           And the shared interpretation:

                              Two observers both hold the same six-bit b ∈ F₂⁶ .

                              Each one draws the cube corresponding to that b .

                              If the closure holds — ∂(b) = 0000 — the six face diagonals close, the cube is "solid,"
                              and both observers see the same shape.

                              If the closure fails — ∂(b) ≠ 0 — the odd vertex is visible as a missing or doubled
                              diagonal, and both observers can see which relation is missing.

                              The cube's spatial resolution exposes the closure failure visually.

                           That is the abstract semantic bridge: the cube is what the closure looks like.


                           The calc loop as the spatial enumeration

                           Your calc walks exactly this cube:

                              diagonal is the XOR of the six face readings. This is the block's accumulated
                              difference — the relation state.

                              linear is the sum. This is the position along the cube's axis — the spatial coordinate.

                           reading (sum). Both are stored in the ruler:

                             js


                             rule[6] = linear;
                             rule[7] = diagonal;


                           And the closure rules are:

                             js


                             case (xy ^ diagonal) === 0:
                             case diagonal % xy === 0:


                           The first is the exact XOR closure. The second is the divisibility closure. Together they
                           define when the cube is "solid" — when the six faces align.

                             swap64    large slice        8-byte reflection

                           the answer.


                           The shared interpretation

                           Two observers, same block, same cube:

                           spatial resolution. They are the same object, read two ways, and the closure is what
                           makes the reading shared — because two observers can only agree on a shape if the
                           shape is well-formed, and well-formedness is the XOR closure.
